tagline: From Skagit farmland to shoreline bends on a former through highway.
intro: Chuckanut Drive crosses Skagit Valley farmland before winding along the shore toward Bellingham, with views of the San Juan Islands. The road is generally two lanes wide, with narrow shoulders and a pair of hairpin turns at Oyster Creek. It is a Washington state scenic byway; State of Washington Tourism highlights its farmland, shoreline and water views, and gives the 20-mile drive an hour. Between Burlington and Bow-Edison, the approach runs past a patchwork of fields. Bow and Edison sit off the drive at Bow Junction, before the coastal section.

The route began as an 1890s logging road connecting the Skagit Valley with Bellingham. It opened as a gravel section of the Pacific Highway in spring 1916 and was paved in 1921. The Pacific Highway became US 99 in 1926. When the main highway shifted inland via Lake Samish in 1931, Chuckanut Drive became US 99 Alternate.

From I-5 north of Burlington, SR 11 travels northwest to Bow and Edison at the head of Samish Bay. It follows the bay around Blanchard Mountain, passes through Larrabee State Park, then follows Chuckanut Bay. The drive descends into Fairhaven on Bellingham Bay before SR 11 turns east to rejoin I-5.

moments.title: Edison
moments.text: Edison once served as headquarters for a project with a national audience: Equality Colony. The Brotherhood of the Cooperative Commonwealth backed the socialist settlement in 1897. On 280 acres outside town, members farmed and milled timber, with a school and shops for blacksmithing and copper work. Their newspaper, Industrial Freedom, circulated nationally. The community folded shortly after 1903. Edison now has a concentration of artists and galleries. The village was named for inventor Thomas Alva Edison. Edison’s compact main street has galleries and places to eat; Bow and Edison are both off Chuckanut Drive at Bow Junction.

moments.title: Samish Bay
moments.text: At Samish Bay, Chuckanut Drive turns from farmland toward the mountain shore. Near Blanchard it crosses the railroad, then follows the west side of Blanchard Mountain at the southern end of the Chuckanut Mountains. The railroad beside the farmland approach is the BNSF Bellingham Subdivision. Amtrak’s Cascades passenger trains use it too, sharing this coastal approach with the highway. A local artist installed a Loch Ness Monster sculpture in the bay during the 2010s; it is visible from the road. Farther along, the road passes an oyster farm before negotiating two hairpin turns at Oyster Creek.

moments.title: Larrabee State Park
moments.text: Washington’s first state park began with an offer of waterfront land along Chuckanut Drive. Governor Ernest Lister proposed the park in 1913, and Charles Larrabee agreed to provide the property. Larrabee died the next year; his wife Frances completed the donation. Accepted by the state in 1915, it was first called Chuckanut State Park and renamed Larrabee in 1923. In 1936, Works Progress Administration funding helped add a water system, playground equipment and kitchen shelters. The following year, the Larrabee family donated another 1,500 acres. Clayton Beach has sandstone formations and tidepools, with views across Samish Bay toward the San Juan Islands.
